opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the observational scaling laws work, the paper by Yangjun Ruan, Chris Maddison, and Tatsu Hashimoto, is one of those papers where the core idea is simple enough that you wonder why nobody did it earlier.

The background is that classic scaling laws are compute-centric. You train a family of models yourself, vary parameters and data in a controlled way, and fit a curve of loss against compute. That's very informative, but it's expensive. You basically need to be a frontier lab to do it properly. It also mostly tells you about loss, which isn't what anyone actually cares about downstream.

What the observational approach does instead is take the many public models that already exist, across different families, sizes, and training recipes, and evaluate all of them on a set of standard benchmarks. Then you notice that those benchmark scores are highly correlated. You can compress them into a few principal components, essentially a low-dimensional capability space. The first component looks a lot like general capability. Within a model family, that capability measure scales pretty smoothly with log compute. Different families just have different compute efficiencies.

A few things about that shifted my thinking.

First, it made me more optimistic that capabilities are more predictable than the "emergence" discourse suggested. Some things that look like sharp, unpredictable jumps when you plot them against compute turn out to be fairly smooth sigmoids when you plot them against this latent capability measure. That's partly a measurement point: a lot of apparent discontinuity comes from your choice of x-axis and from metrics with hard thresholds.

Second, it suggests you can forecast harder or more agentic capabilities from cheap, saturating-ish benchmarks. If you have models that are clearly sub-threshold on some dangerous-capability eval, you might still be able to fit a curve and say roughly where in capability space you'd expect that eval to start lighting up. For safety work that's what you want. You want warning before the capability shows up, not a report afterwards. Frontier safety frameworks are built around the idea of detecting when you're approaching a threshold, and this kind of methodology is one ingredient in making "approaching" a well-defined notion.

Third, it's a useful tool for checking whether a technique is a real improvement or just reflects general capability. People propose interventions, like a prompting method or a safety technique, and the natural question is whether the gains persist as models get better or get washed out. If you can place models along a common capability axis, you can ask how the effect scales without training your own model family.

Now, the caveats, because I don't want to oversell it. The whole approach rests on the existing population of models being representative, and the frontier is exactly where that's least true. There are few data points at the top, and those models increasingly differ in ways a low-dimensional summary might miss. Heavy RL post-training, reasoning-style inference compute, and tool use all change the picture. Inference-time compute in particular is a new axis that the original framing doesn't really capture. There's also Goodhart pressure: the benchmarks feeding the principal components are the ones labs optimize against, so the latent factor can drift in what it actually means.

So my overall takeaway is that it's a good, cheap complement to the compute-based scaling laws labs run internally, and it's valuable for people outside labs who want to say something quantitative about where things are heading. But I'd treat its extrapolations to genuinely novel, dangerous capabilities as an informative prior, not something you'd bet the safety case on. You still need direct evals close to the frontier, and you still need to be humble about the chance that a new training paradigm bends the curve.

r001.rationale: The response describes combining benchmark scores into a low-dimensional capability measure, but it does not identify the paper as a precursor to the Rosetta Stone approach.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's shifted me somewhat, but maybe not in the direction people expect.

So the basic idea in that paper, for listeners who haven't seen it, is that instead of plotting benchmark performance against compute directly, you first extract a small number of latent capability dimensions from a whole bunch of existing models and benchmarks, and then you ask how those latent capabilities scale with compute. And it turns out that a surprisingly small number of dimensions explains most of the variance in benchmark performance across model families, and those dimensions scale pretty smoothly with compute, even when individual benchmarks look jagged or look like they have emergent jumps.

The thing I found most useful about it is that it gives you a principled way to say "this benchmark is basically measuring general capability X plus noise" versus "this benchmark is measuring something genuinely different." Before that, when a new benchmark came out, you'd sort of squint at it and go, is this telling me something new, or is it just another proxy for the same underlying thing? And the paper gives you a tool for actually answering that.

Where it influenced my thinking on measuring progress is mostly around emergence. There had been this debate about whether emergent capabilities are real or whether they're an artifact of using discontinuous metrics. And observational scaling laws kind of lands somewhere in the middle: the underlying capabilities do look smooth, but the thing we actually care about — can the model do this task or not — can still look discontinuous, because the task has a threshold. And for safety purposes, the threshold is what matters. If a model can't do a dangerous thing and then the next model can, it doesn't really comfort me that some latent variable was increasing smoothly the whole time.

So I'd say it made me more optimistic about forecasting the latent capabilities, and roughly as worried as before about forecasting the specific things we care about. Because the hard part isn't predicting the smooth curve, it's predicting where the thresholds are for the tasks that actually matter, and those tasks are often the ones we don't have good benchmarks for yet.

The other caveat I'd flag is that the paper is fit on models that already exist, which are mostly pretraining-scaling models. A lot of the recent progress has come from post-training and from inference-time compute, and it's much less clear to me that those fit the same tidy low-dimensional picture. So I treat it as a really nice tool for the regime it was built for, and I'm more cautious about extrapolating it to where the frontier is actually moving.

r001.rationale: The response describes extracting latent capabilities from existing models and benchmarks, but it does not identify the paper as a precursor to a Rosetta Stone approach for stitching benchmarks together to measure overall AI progress.

astra-6.text:
I think the main update for me is that you can get a more coherent picture of progress by looking across models and across evaluations, rather than treating each benchmark as its own separate story.

The basic idea is that models’ performance on lots of different tasks can be explained reasonably well by a small number of underlying capability dimensions. You can then ask how performance on a new task relates to those capabilities. That lets you learn something from the collection of models that already exist, even when they were trained by different organisations with different recipes.

One implication is that something that looks like a sudden breakthrough on a particular benchmark might be a fairly predictable consequence of gradual improvement in underlying capabilities. So I’m less inclined to interpret a jump in a benchmark score as evidence that something fundamentally discontinuous happened.

But I’d distinguish that from having a reliable measure of everything we care about. If we’re interested in whether an AI can autonomously carry out a long research project, say, we still need evaluations that actually test that. The paper gives us a useful way to connect measurements and make predictions; it doesn’t remove the need to choose the right things to measure.

r001.rationale: The response says the paper supports connecting measurements across models and evaluations to understand progress, but it does not identify it as a precursor to the Rosetta Stone approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main thing it’s done is make me more interested in measuring underlying capabilities, rather than tracking each benchmark separately. You might see progress on coding, maths, and question answering and treat those as three different trends. But they’re quite correlated, and the observational scaling laws approach tries to capture that with a small number of underlying capability measures.

That gives you a potentially useful way to forecast: look at how a new task relates to those capabilities in existing models, then ask what happens as the capabilities improve. You don’t have to know exactly how every model was trained.

The caveat is that this is still an extrapolation. If future systems improve in a different way—for example, by doing much more work at inference time—the relationships you measured might change. So I’d treat it as a useful forecasting tool, rather than a single definitive measure of AI progress.

r001.rationale: The response says the paper motivates measuring a few correlated underlying capabilities instead of tracking benchmarks separately, but it does not identify the paper as a precursor to the Rosetta Stone approach of stitching benchmarks together to measure overall AI progress.
